# Selection — TRD §15 row 5: the finalization shape

**Status:** selected, and folded into the TRD. **Date:** 2026-08-19
**Closes:** TRD §15 row 5 · **Scope of:** review 3b (protocol)
**Constrained by:** TRD §7.4, §7.5, §7.6, §13.5, §13.7 · PRD §6.5 · **Stage:** [sequencing.md](../sequencing.md) §3.5
**Vectors:** [`test/vectors/finalization.json`](../../test/vectors/finalization.json), generated by
[`scripts/generate-finalization-vectors.mjs`](../../scripts/generate-finalization-vectors.mjs)
**Companions:** [row 1](./row-1-algorithm-suite.md) selects SHA-256 and Ed25519 and carries their published KATs;
[row 3](./row-3-record-format.md) established the length-prefix and binding conventions followed here;
[row 11](./row-11-enrollment-ceremony.md) is the other half of what a hostile service must not be able to do.

---

## The selection

```
The accepted chain          one per (workspace, credential)

  link_n = SHA-256( LP("done/accept/v1") || LP(workspace_id) || LP(credential_id)
                    || LP(dec n) || LP(dec epoch_n) || LP(hex digest_n)
                    || LP(hex link_(n-1)) )

  link_0   32 zero bytes — the empty chain. Position 1 still binds the label,
           the workspace and the credential, so an empty chain is not a shared
           starting value.
  digest_n the envelope's update digest, already in the clear for the relay to
           validate (§7.4). The chain introduces no new cleartext field.

The signed head             amortized over a batch, not one per envelope

  Head_n = Ed25519( K_accept ;
             LP("done/accept-head/v1") || LP(workspace_id) || LP(credential_id)
             || LP(dec n) || LP(hex link_n) || LP(dec epoch) || LP(final) )

  final    "true" | "false". True is the finalization boundary: no position
           above n will ever be accepted for this credential.
  K_accept a separate acceptance-signing key, certified by the authorization
           key in the epoch it appears in. It is hot, because it signs on the
           delivery path. The epoch key is not, and that is the point of
           splitting them.

The client's four rules

  1. Verify a head against the link you replayed yourself, never against the
     link the head claims.
  2. Admit no envelope without a signed head at or above its position.
  3. First-seen-wins per (credential, position). A second link at a position
     you already hold is equivocation, and a valid signature is not an answer
     to it.
  4. Above the newest head, hold rather than discard. Missing evidence is
     availability, not integrity (§7.5).

Two carriers gain the same field

  Epoch payload       the head vector — (credential, n, link) for every
                      credential, as of that epoch. §13.5 already binds which
                      credentials exist; this binds where each had got to.
  Checkpoint manifest the same vector, so a device starting from a checkpoint
                      verifies the suffix forward from authenticated heads
                      rather than replaying from genesis (§7.6).

                LP(s) = uint16be(byteLength(utf8 s)) || utf8 s
```

Everything below is why, and what it cost.

---

## 1. The three candidates were not three

Before the fold, §7.5 offered per-envelope receipts, an append-only accepted log with inclusion proofs, and a
checkpoint plus an authenticated suffix — and said the middle "is the closest fit to structures already
required". Designing it rather than picking it turns up that **the second and third are one construction at two
cadences, and the first is that construction with the property removed.**

| The candidate §7.5 listed            | What it is, once written out                                                 |
| ------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Per-envelope receipts                | A head at every position, and **no chain** — so the receipts are independent |
| Append-only log with proofs          | The chain, with heads at whatever cadence the service chooses                |
| Checkpoint plus authenticated suffix | The same chain, with the checkpoint carrying the head vector for the prefix  |

So the real choice was never three-way. It was **whether the evidence for position _n_ says anything about
position _n-1_**, and everything else is a cadence parameter.

**That reframing is worth more than the selection it produces**, because it is what makes the third candidate
stop looking like a rival and start looking like §7.6's manifest doing its job. §7.5 already predicted the
composition; what was not obvious until the shapes were written side by side is that composing them requires
adding exactly one field to the manifest, and the same field to the epoch.

---

## 2. What an independent receipt cannot do, stated as the attack

A receipt says _the service accepted this envelope_. A hostile relay holding a bag of valid receipts may show
any subset of them, and **every subset is as well-formed as the whole**. That is not a subtle failure:

1. A credential writes envelopes at positions 1 through 20; the service accepts all twenty and issues twenty
   receipts.
2. The relay delivers 1, 2, 3 and 20 to a device, withholding the middle sixteen.
3. Every receipt verifies. The device has no expression for _something is missing_, because nothing it holds
   refers to anything it does not hold.

**A chain has no subsets.** Position 20's link is a function of position 19's, so a device that can recompute
link 20 has necessarily seen 1 through 19. The gap in step 2 becomes an arithmetic failure rather than an
absence nobody can name.

**This is the same argument §7.5 makes against a numeric high-water mark, one level along.** A high-water mark
is a claim about a count; a receipt is a claim about one item; neither is a claim about a _set_. The chain is
the smallest object that makes a claim about a set, which is what "accepted set" was asking for all along.

---

## 3. The head is amortized, and that is what makes evidence-on-everything affordable

§7.5 requires evidence on **every** applied envelope. Read naively that is one service signature per envelope,
which is candidate 1's cost and puts an asymmetric signature on the delivery path at write rates.

**The chain decouples the two.** One signed head at position _n_ is evidence for every position at or below
_n_, because the client recomputes the chain to get there. The service may sign per envelope, per delivery
batch, or per second; **the security property does not change with the cadence, only the hold latency does**
(§5).

**One consequence is not negotiable, and it is rule 1.** The client verifies a head against the link it
replayed itself, never against the link the head carries. Those sound equivalent and are not: a client that
trusts the head's own link field has a signature over a value it never checked against its own history, and the
chain is then decorative. The vectors make this concrete — `head-wrong-link` is a _genuinely signed_ head over a
different link at the same position, and the only thing that refuses it is the client having computed its own.

---

## 4. Non-equivocation, and the bound that has to be stated

§7.5 requires the accepted stream to be **non-equivocating from a client's point of view**. The chain gives
that within one client's view, by rule 3: once a client holds a link at (credential, position), a different
link there is refused no matter how well signed. What it does not give, and what no construction here gives, is
protection against a **split view**.

**The bound, stated in §13.5's own manner rather than left to be discovered.** A service that maintains two
consistent forks and shows each device only its own fork equivocates undetectably by cryptographic means alone.
Detection requires two views to meet. Three things make them meet in this product, and none of them is a proof:

- **The epoch binds the head vector.** Epochs are serialized by the service and clients reject ancestors
  (§13.5, §11.2 test 4), so sustaining a fork means forking the authorization lineage too — a much louder act
  than withholding an envelope, and one §7.3's authorization-reconciles-before-content rule puts in front of
  every session.
- **Checkpoints carry the same vector**, so a device restoring from the durable store compares a head vector it
  did not fetch in this session.
- **Divergent content is the user-visible symptom**, and this product's whole claim is that the phone and the
  laptop agree. A fork that is never detected cryptographically is a fork the person watches happen.

**What is deliberately not selected is a transparency log or client gossip.** Either would close the split view
properly, and both are a larger commitment than anything else in this design — a second serialization authority
with its own availability and retention story, for a product whose workspace typically has two devices and one
person. **The honest statement is therefore the one §13.5 already models for rollback: the protection is
bounded, and the bound is that it holds within a view and detects across views rather than preventing forks.**
Overclaiming here is easy, because "non-equivocating" is true of the per-credential chain and reads as though it
were true of the service.

---

## 5. What this puts on the delivery path, including one budget that does not exist

**The acceptance signer is hot, and cannot be a batch component.** Evidence is required before a client applies
anything, so whatever signs heads is in the request path. That is a real constraint on §7.3's component split —
"the authorization service issues acceptance evidence" is a sentence about an online service, not a nightly job.
**Splitting `K_accept` from the epoch-signing key is the whole mitigation**: the key that must live on a hot
path signs only _this envelope reached position n_, and the key that admits and revokes credentials does not
have to be there at all. Rotating `K_accept` is then an ordinary epoch event, because the epoch is what
certifies it.

**Rule 4 introduces a latency §12 has no row for.** An envelope arriving ahead of the head that covers it is
held, so **remote edit → visible** is bounded below by the head cadence, not by the network. §12 budgets
`envelope verify on receipt < 2 ms p95` — which this comfortably meets, at one SHA-256 per envelope and one
amortized Ed25519 verify — but that row measures the wrong thing for this design. **The missing row is
`remote edit → visible on the second device`, and its dominant term is a service parameter rather than a client
one.** Naming it here because it is exactly the shape of budget that gets discovered after it is missed: the
client is fast, every existing row is green, and the product feels slow.

**Retention is row 6's and is bounded by this.** A device retains its own outbound envelopes back to the last
checkpoint it has seen admitted (§7.4); the chain adds that it must retain enough of its own links to replay
forward from the newest head vector it trusts. Both bounds move together, which is the useful part — row 6
inherits one number rather than two.

---

## 6. What it costs

| Cost                      | Size                                                                                                  |
| ------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Per envelope, on the wire | 32 bytes of link. Nothing else — `digest`, `epoch` and the credential are already there (§7.4)        |
| Per envelope, client CPU  | One SHA-256 over about 200 bytes                                                                      |
| Per head                  | One Ed25519 signature by the service, one verify by each client                                       |
| Per epoch                 | The head vector: 32 bytes plus a position per credential. A two-device workspace pays under 100 bytes |
| Per checkpoint manifest   | The same vector                                                                                       |
| Bundle                    | **Nothing.** SHA-256 and Ed25519 are WebCrypto (row 1)                                                |

**No bundle cost is worth stating plainly, because the headroom is contested.** [performance.md](../performance.md)
records 43.7 kB of gzipped headroom against §12's 350 kB, and row 2's WASM candidate for the measured journal
breach wants 24.3 kB of it. A protocol row that needed a library would be competing with a fix for a defect,
and this one does not.

---

## 7. What Stage 4 owes, and what is not in this row

**Two carriers gain a field, and both are cheaper to change now than later** — but neither is on-disk, so
§2.1's deadline does not apply and this is a Stage 4 obligation rather than a Stage 1 one. The epoch payload
and the checkpoint manifest each gain the head vector, and §13.5's payload list and §7.6's representation list
should say so before either is built.

**The excluded credential must still be told** (§13.7), and `final: true` is what tells it. A revoked device
can verify the head that closes its own chain — the signature is over public material and needs no content key
— so _the workspace stopped accepting your writes at position n_ is a statement it can check rather than infer
from silence. That is the honesty requirement §13.7 flags as easy to miss, satisfied by a field that had to
exist anyway.

**Not in this row.** How a link and a head travel beside an envelope is **row 4**'s framing. How deep a device
keeps its own chain is **row 6**. The checkpoint's own construction, and how the head vector is carried inside
it, is **row 7**. Chain-head discovery for a brand-new device is **row 9**, and it is the row this one leans on
hardest: everything above assumes the client knows which head is current, and §13.5 already records that a
brand-new client trusts the service for that with no mechanism to fix it.

---

## 8. The vectors

`node scripts/generate-finalization-vectors.mjs` writes them; `--check` fails if they are stale, and
`pnpm check` now runs it with the other eight.

**The primitive KATs are not here, and their absence is structural** — SHA-256 and Ed25519 are row 1's, and
[row 1's vectors](../../test/vectors/algorithm-suite.json) carry FIPS 180-4 and RFC 8032. What this file carries
is composition.

**Four chain vectors and two heads.** Three positions from a laptop across an epoch boundary, plus the phone at
_its_ position 1 carrying the laptop's position-1 digest — same workspace, same position, same bytes, different
chain, which is the per-credential split made visible. Then a live head at position 2 and a finalized head at
position 3.

**The keys are RFC 8032 §7.1's**, TEST 2 signing and TEST 1 as the impostor, and the generator proves each pair
to itself before writing. Row 14's rule: a vector binding a public key to a private one proves nothing if its
own halves are unrelated.

**Seventeen negatives** — every field of both constructions, plus the two client rules that are not field
bindings. `forked-link-at-same-position` is a _properly signed_ second head over a different link at a position
the client already holds, and `envelope-beyond-signed-head` is the hold rule. A rule nobody runs is a sentence.

**One thing the coverage audit reported, and it is a finding rather than a fix.** `pnpm vectors:coverage` elides
each bound field and watches which negatives stop failing, and the rule adopted in
[decisions.md](../decisions.md) is that a negative named `aad-only-*` must be rescued by exactly one field. **The
first link negative named that way failed the check, correctly**: eliding the _head's_ `link` field rescues
**every** link-layer negative at once, because that field is the only thing tying the two layers together.

That is not a coverage gap and it is not a defect in the construction — it is what a two-layer construction
looks like to an audit built for single-layer AEADs, and this is the first two-layer construction in the tree.
The negative is renamed rather than the audit weakened, and the observation is worth keeping: **`accepted
head.link` is the pin.** Remove it and the chain still computes, every published vector still round-trips, and
nothing in the system is checking history any more. There is no better single sentence for what a reviewer
should look at first.
